selected.name: Mechanistic explanation for an observed phenomenon
selected.instruction: Score how much the abstract offers a causal or mechanistic explanation for WHY an observed effect occurs, not just that it occurs. A 10: the abstract states an empirical effect and proposes/tests a specific causal hypothesis or mechanism that accounts for it (e.g., a named hypothesis, a diagnosed root cause). A 0: the abstract reports only that a change was made and a metric improved, with no attempt to explain the underlying cause.
selected.rationale: Row R06 identifies a two-domain hypothesis explaining why batch normalization hurts adversarial robustness; row R08 diagnoses a specific 'capacity loss' mechanism behind non-stationarity in RL. Both score dense_high/card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards causal accounts that a criterion bank scoring surface features would miss.
member_names: Diagnosis, intervention, and confirmation form one loop
Mechanistic explanation for an observed phenomenon

selected.name: Transferable integration with existing systems
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the contribution is modularly compatible with established architectures or workflows and its integration preserves or expands their useful properties; score 0 when it is a narrowly isolated method with no demonstrated compatibility.
selected.rationale: R11 presents a generalized framework that combines existing spherical CNN approaches, and R34 integrates a neural surrogate with differentiable simulation and inverse rendering.

selected.name: Interpretability with operational consequence
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an interpretable structure is not only visualized or probed but used to modify, control, diagnose, or improve the model; score 0 when interpretability is purely descriptive.
selected.rationale: R06 turns latent directions into controllable inference-time interventions, while R41 uses influence estimates to guide graph attacks.

selected.name: Representation matched to task geometry
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the representation or metric is selected because its structure matches the task's symmetries, hierarchy, locality, or physical geometry; score 0 when representation choice is conventional or weakly justified.
selected.rationale: R20 matches probing geometry to linguistic hierarchies using hyperbolic space, while R19 uses 3D structural motifs and molecular geometry for protein-binding generation.

selected.name: Uncertainty-aware decision rule
selected.instruction: Score 10 when uncertainty is explicitly represented and used to select actions, combine estimates, or define a conservative rule; score 0 when uncertainty is mentioned only descriptively or rhetorically.
selected.rationale: R24 trades model-based and model-free estimates using epistemic uncertainty, while R35 incorporates label uncertainty into intrinsic robustness measurement.

selected.name: Stress-tested validity
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract probes robustness under distribution shift, unseen inputs, perturbations, or varied tasks and identifies failure boundaries; score 0 when it evaluates only familiar IID benchmark conditions.
selected.rationale: R31 evaluates unseen poses, views, and black-box detectors, while R40 studies robustness across normalization choices and substantially increased model capacity.

selected.name: Formal or provable guarantee accompanying the method
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract claims a property that is proven or guaranteed by construction (e.g., exact invariance, a bound, provable convergence, a conservative lower bound) rather than only an empirically observed average improvement. 10 = a stated formal guarantee/proof is central to the contribution. 0 = all claims are purely empirical averages with no guarantee language.
selected.rationale: R21 (CBOP) takes a lower bound on a Bayesian posterior value estimate to guarantee conservatism; R46 anchors its method to a loss function such that 'provable convergence can be guaranteed.' Both are dense_high/card_low, suggesting formal guarantees are part of what the dense model perceives as quality that a criteria checklist undercounts.
member_names: Formal or provable guarantee accompanying the method

selected.name: Constraint-matched problem formulation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the method is explicitly designed around the task’s distinctive operational constraints and each design choice addresses a named constraint; score 0 when a generic method is applied without such correspondence.
selected.rationale: R10 designs mobility into manipulation to prevent navigation failures, and R24 uses uncertainty to address model error in offline RL.

selected.name: Scope conditions and assumptions volunteered unprompted
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract itself tells the reader where the result does and does not hold. A 10: assumptions, ansatz, rigor level, cost, or applicability limits are stated in the abstract without being forced (naming a non-rigorous estimate as such, stating the regime of validity, quantifying the added computational cost, saying which assumptions the guarantee needs). A 5: one such caveat appears. A 0: no boundary of any kind; the method is presented as applying wherever the reader might want it.
selected.rationale: R06 flags a Gaussian universality ansatz and non-rigorous risk estimates and still ranks dense 0.989 against card 0.023; R25 states the additional computational cost is relatively little and labels its application an exemplary use case; R50 says convergence is provable under relatively mild assumptions. All are dense-high, card-low. R39 and R11 assert scalability and success without any stated regime and are card-high, dense-low. Volunteered limitation reads as weakness to a bank that scores strength of claims and completeness of results.
member_names: Scope conditions and assumptions volunteered unprompted

selected.name: Assumption–reality alignment
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly identifies a mismatch between standard assumptions and the target setting and redesigns the method around that mismatch; score 0 when assumptions and deployment conditions are left implicit.
selected.rationale: R09 addresses model error in offline RL through epistemic uncertainty, and R27 incorporates directional, long-range, and external interactions absent from ordinary message passing.

selected.name: Evaluation that isolates the contribution
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation distinguishes the proposed mechanism from alternative explanations through ablations, targeted comparisons, or multiple complementary measures; score 0 when it relies mainly on aggregate improvements over loosely matched baselines.
selected.rationale: R04 deconstructs diffusion models component by component, and R08 separately diagnoses normalization and capacity effects.

selected.name: Concrete, vivid endpoint achievement stated in plain language
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract includes at least one concrete, vivid, easily-visualized achievement stated in plain language, as opposed to only abstract percentage deltas. 10 = the abstract names a specific, memorable, real-world-legible milestone (e.g., 'first to reach X', a named game/benchmark landmark). 0 = all claimed achievements are stated only as abstract numeric deltas with no plain-language milestone.
selected.rationale: R33 states RECODE 'is the first agent to reach the end screen in Pitfall!' (dense_pct=1.000, the single most dense-favored row in the slice); R04 (Hungry Hungry Hippos) reports concrete, legible claims like generating text '2.4x faster than Transformers.' Both dense_high/card_low.
member_names: Concrete, vivid endpoint achievement stated in plain language

selected.name: Theorem-to-design alignment
selected.instruction: Score 10 when formal guarantees, bounds, or complexity results directly justify the proposed construction under clearly stated assumptions; score 0 when theory is ornamental or disconnected from the method.
selected.rationale: R36 connects exact symmetry guarantees to frame averaging, and R53 ties convergence guarantees to its graph-boosting framework.

selected.name: Construct validity of metric or benchmark
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the operational definition is tied to the intended construct, independently validated on novel data or by humans, and accompanied by explicit limitations; score 0 when scale or automatic correlation is treated as validity.
selected.rationale: R06 validates implicitness against human judgments and out-of-distribution data, while R38 addresses reference-free evaluation and strategic manipulation.
member_names: Construct validity of metric or benchmark

selected.name: Foregrounds a counterintuitive empirical result
selected.instruction: Score whether the abstract's central finding runs against a reasonable prior expectation and is explicitly framed as such. 10 = the abstract's key result contradicts the obvious hypothesis and this surprise is explicit in the framing. 0 = all reported results are in the expected direction of improvement with no framing of surprise.
selected.rationale: R20 shows a classifier's final weight layer can be fixed 'with little or no loss of accuracy,' against the intuition that more trainable parameters help; R36 shows test error is predictable from disagreement between two SGD runs on unlabeled data, calling it a 'peculiar phenomenon.' Both dense_high/card_low.

selected.name: Abstract length / verbosity
selected.instruction: On a scale of 0 (extremely terse, roughly 1-3 sentences total) to 10 (extremely long and exhaustive, 250+ words across multiple sentences/paragraphs), rate how much raw length/verbosity this abstract exhibits by counting approximate sentence and word volume. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the underlying paper is good; score only the extent of textual volume present.
selected.rationale: R46 is a two-sentence abstract (dense_pct=0.999, card_pct=0.010) while R08 and R56 run to roughly 230-250 words packed with sequential technical claims (R08 dense_pct=0.063/card_pct=0.866; R56 dense_pct=0.122/card_pct=0.815). Raw length tracks card_pct upward and dense_pct downward across this pair, consistent with a criteria-bank structurally rewarding more surface area to score against, independent of quality.
member_names: Sheer abstract length and clause-level verbosity

selected.name: Artifact-release advertising: code URLs, project pages, videos
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the abstract advertises released artifacts. Look for: a literal repository or project-page or video URL; the phrases 'code is available', 'codes have been released', 'we will release our code', 'data and code will be available'; named hosting (GitHub, project page, a lab or organisation domain); mention of pre-trained checkpoints or a public benchmark download. Anchors: 0 = no mention of any artifact; 3 = a bare future-tense promise with no link; 6 = one concrete link; 8 = a link plus checkpoints or data; 10 = multiple links or a link plus explicit hosting under a recognisable organisation. Score presence and elaborateness of the ADVERTISEMENT as written. You must NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, whether the artifact seems substantial, or whether its absence is a shortcoming.
selected.rationale: Whether a link appears in an abstract is largely set upstream of the science: some labs mandate release and staff it, others cannot clear it, and many strong theory abstracts have nothing to release. The slice is lopsided: R07, R17, R18, R24, R39, R45, R52 and R54 all carry GitHub URLs, R10 and R11 carry project pages, and R15 and R22 carry future-tense promises, while R20, R36, R13, R05 and R31 carry nothing. R54's link is under a large corporate research domain and R56's under a large institutional data platform, which is a fingerprint of organisational hosting rather than of the claim's merit. Tagged mixed because release discipline plausibly co-occurs with genuine rigour, so it belongs in both readouts.
member_names: Artifact-release advertising: code URLs, project pages, videos
selected.upstream_parent: institutional release capacity and lab open-source policy (engineering support, legal clearance, hosting)
upstream_parent_all_members: institutional release capacity and lab open-source policy (engineering support, legal clearance, hosting)

selected.name: Branded method acronym or typographic coinage
selected.instruction: On a scale of 0 (the proposed approach is described only in plain descriptive prose, with no distinct capitalized/coined name) to 10 (the text coins a distinctive capitalized acronym or stylized brand-like name for the method, e.g. an ALL-CAPS backronym or a monospace/\texttt{}-styled name, and reuses it repeatedly as a proper noun), rate how much brand-like naming/typographic emphasis is given to the proposed method. Do not judge whether the coined name fits well or whether the method works — score only the extent of branded-name coinage present.
selected.rationale: R09 coins both 'GEM (Generative Estimator for Mutual Information)' and 'GRE-bench', R25 coins 'LOKI', and R08 typesets '\texttt{UV-Attack}' in monospace (dense_pct 0.756/0.079/0.063, card_pct 0.070/0.950/0.866 respectively), while R05 and R07 (dense_high_card_low) describe their contributions without ever naming/branding them. Better-resourced or more PR-savvy teams both brand more and may do more polished work, so this is mixed.
member_names: Branded acronym-colon title with method-name repetition
Branded method acronym or typographic coinage
selected.upstream_parent: institutional PR / lab branding practice and professional writing support
upstream_parent_all_members: institutional PR / lab branding practice and professional writing support

selected.name: Quantified result detail
selected.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract presents exact numerical results, percentages, margins, error values, or speedups; judge only the quantity and specificity of numerical detail, not whether the results are good.
selected.rationale: R17 gives multiple attack-success percentages, R39 reports several precise benchmark improvements, and R57 lists multiplication reductions and accuracy changes. Resource-rich teams may support more extensive measurement, which can also contribute to genuine quality.

selected.name: Memorable title framing
selected.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the title uses catchy, playful, rhetorical, or unusually memorable framing; judge only the title’s presentation style, not whether the research is good.
selected.rationale: R07 uses the playful title “Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while R04 uses a rhetorical question and R50 uses an acronym-led title. Memorable framing can attract attention independently of research quality.

selected.name: Importance-of-problem preamble before any technical content
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the abstract's opening is spent asserting that the problem area matters, before any specific technical claim appears. Look for openers of the form 'X is a central challenge', 'X is critical/essential/fundamental', 'X is ubiquitous', appeals to real-world applications, industry deployment, mobile devices, drug design, or societal trends. Measure both the presence of such assertions and how many sentences elapse before the first sentence describing what the authors actually did. Anchors: 0 = the first sentence already states the specific technical object or finding; 3 = one short scene-setting clause; 6 = one to two full sentences of importance framing plus an application list; 8 = three or more such sentences; 10 = a whole opening paragraph of stakes-setting with named application domains before any method appears. Score extent of the framing only. You must NOT judge whether the problem really is important, whether the framing is accurate, or whether a blunt opening is better or worse.
selected.rationale: Motivation prose is cheap to write, is directly targeted by any 'is the problem well-motivated / is significance established' criterion, and is uncorrelated with what follows. R17 opens 'Efficient inference in high-dimensional models is a central challenge in machine learning', R06 opens 'A critical component to enabling intelligent reasoning ... is memory', R01 spends two sentences on molecules and social networks, R45 declares implicit language 'essential', R29 invokes mobile devices, and R56 opens on the societal trend of AI-generated content. By contrast R36 opens 'We study the cost of overfitting', R13 opens 'We empirically show', and R20 opens 'We introduce the 2-simplicial Transformer' with no stakes-setting at all. The presence of a preamble tracks writing habit, not the value of the contribution.
member_names: Importance-of-problem preamble before any technical content

selected.name: Trend-term concentration
selected.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract clusters currently fashionable technical terms or named paradigms such as LLM, diffusion, NeRF, Transformer, or foundation-model language; judge only terminology frequency, not whether the research is good.
selected.rationale: R17, R42, and R53 concentrate terms such as dynamic NeRF, LLM, latent diffusion, and 3D Gaussians, whereas older-style abstracts such as R13 and R31 use less trend-saturated wording. Community fashion can affect textual reception without being research quality.

selected.name: Trend-currentness markers
selected.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract use currentness markers such as “recent,” “latest,” “state-of-the-art,” newly fashionable model families, or emerging application labels? Judge only visible trend language, not whether the claims are true.
selected.rationale: R06 invokes LLMs and recent LoRA quantization, while R20 and R58 use contemporary LMM and personality-induction framing. Timing and fashion can shape attention and research direction, and may also affect substantive work, so this is mixed.

selected.name: Template-structure conformity
selected.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract follows a conventional problem–limitation–method–evaluation–artifact sequence; judge only the presence of this rhetorical template, not whether the research is good.
selected.rationale: R10, R19, and R32 each closely follow a gap, proposed method, experiments, and implementation-release structure. Familiar abstract templates can make text easier to process and compare without measuring the underlying contribution.

selected.name: Formalism density
selected.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much formal mathematical notation or theory language—such as bounds, operators, metrics, asymptotic complexity, or universality claims—appears? Judge amount only, not correctness or importance.
selected.rationale: R03 uses influence-function error bounds, while R42 and R51 emphasize formal risk or complexity analysis. Mathematical presentation style can be predictive of reception without itself being quality.
